quote: then I suspect that the point at which the average person will actually start to grant credence overriding their initial impression, purely because of academic credentials, is somewhere around the Nobel Laureate level
content: Hovland & Weiss's own follow-up measured the effect that matters. After four weeks the credibility advantage had disappeared: messages from low-credibility sources gained agreement and those from high-credibility sources lost it. That is the "sleeper effect" (Hovland & Weiss 1951). What the essay describes, credentials overriding a durable first impression of a claim that "sounds wrong," was tested head-on. People counted a scientist with elite credentials and National Academy membership as an expert only when his stated position matched their cultural predisposition (Kahan, Jenkins-Smith & Braman 2011). The credential was ignored when the claim clashed with their prior view. Thiel and Kurzweil are the "beyond the mundane" level the essay names, so the institute's experience confirms its threshold.

quote: But did the same people who said, “Come back when you have a PhD,” actually change their minds at all about molecular nanotechnology? Not so far as I ever heard.
content: Smalley's "fat fingers" were aimed at a design Nanosystems does not propose. Drexler's open reply in the same exchange pointed out that his mechanosynthesis positions reactive molecules and uses no manipulator fingers, and Smalley's rejoinder changed the subject to enzymes. The 2006 National Research Council review did not find molecular manufacturing infeasible. It concluded that theoretical analysis could not settle the question and recommended experimental research. The essay's list of "true sources" also includes "uncommon, but well-supported, scientific knowledge or math," "zeitgeists inherited from a profession (that may have good reason for it)," and "patterns perceptually recognized from experience." Those are cases where the other party knows something you do not, which is the "better argument" Fable says is missing. The list is headed as a question "both disagreers should surely be asking themselves."

quote: It has similarly been a general rule with the Machine Intelligence Research Institute that, whatever it is we’re supposed to do to be more credible, when we actually do it, nothing much changes.
content: OpenCog was launched with the institute's sponsorship while Goertzel was its Director of Research, so it was the institute's code effort, not a substitute for one. The later history then ran the test Fable wants. The credential, code and PhD objections did not move anyone. What changed minds was the thing the essay suspected lay underneath, "this matches science fiction," dissolving when real systems became capable. In May 2023 Hinton, Bengio and hundreds of other AI researchers signed a one-sentence statement that mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority (Center for AI Safety, "Statement on AI Risk"). No new doctorate, no new code base. The world changed, and the true rejection went with it.
